title: How Bats Work
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain how bats work: their classification into megabats and microbats, wing structure that differs from birds, flight launched from hanging upside down, echolocation (including Doppler effect and ear folds), torpor and energy-saving sleep, roosting and maternity colonies, ecological benefits such as insect eating and pollination, guano and gunpowder history, vampire bats, white-nose fungus, rabies misconceptions and bat culling, and the World War II bat bomb project. The episode ends with listener mail about a live show and a Nazi Long Island invasion episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and bat appearance
segments.summary: The hosts open with jokes about dolphin running shorts, express fondness for bats, and discuss how bats look cute or frightening, including the micro bats with crazy nostrils and the flying fox.

segments.title: Bat classification and mammal status
segments.summary: Bats are the only flying mammals and belong to the order Chiroptera. They were once split into megabats and microbats by size, but genetic testing has changed the classification, since some small bats are now in the megabat group. Microbats tend to eat insects while megabats mostly eat plants and nectar.

segments.title: Bat disease reservoirs and rabies risk
segments.summary: Bats can carry diseases such as Ebola and rabies because they roost closely together. The hosts note that under one percent of bats are rabid, and that raccoons and skunks are more likely sources of rabies.

segments.title: Bat wing structure and flight
segments.summary: The word for bat in German is a term meaning flying mice. Bat wings are webbed hands with a membrane called the patagium, which differs from bird wings with rigid bones. Bats launch by dropping from a height rather than running or jumping, and they evolved flight from tree-dwelling ancestors.

segments.title: Bat vision and echolocation
segments.summary: Bats are not blind and most have good vision, including color vision according to a German study. Micro bats echolocate, while many fruit-eating bats do not need to. The hosts compare bat echolocation to echoes in a canyon and describe how the bat brain builds a spatial image from sound.

segments.title: How echolocation determines distance, size and direction
segments.summary: Bats judge distance from echo return time, direction from which ear hears the sound first, vertical position from ear folds, and size from echo intensity. They use the Doppler effect to detect whether prey moves toward or away. Bats emit ultrasonic calls, some through the nose.

segments.title: Roosting, torpor and hanging upside down
segments.summary: Vampire bats roost alone or in small groups, while fruit-eating bats gather in colonies of millions. Bats sleep upside down because their tendons lock their claws without muscle energy. Bats enter torpor daily to save energy, cooling their body temperature, and some hibernate.

segments.title: Bat benefits, guano, and vampire bats
segments.summary: Bats eat large numbers of insects, including mosquitoes, and pollinate plants such as bananas, figs, mangoes, and cashews. The Congress Avenue Bridge colony in Austin is a tourist attraction. Guano is a fertilizer and was used for gunpowder in the Civil War. Vampire bats take small amounts of blood from cattle using anticoagulant saliva.

segments.title: Bat reproduction and white-nose fungus
segments.summary: Bats typically have one pup a year, and females may delay fertilization. Females form maternity colonies. White-nose fungus wakes hibernating bats, causing them to starve, with high mortality in some hibernacula. Culling bats for rabies fears and the World War II bat bomb project are also discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail: Washington Square Park live show
segments.summary: A listener writes about attending a live show in Washington Square Park and the New York City show, and about the Nazi U-boat Long Island episode. The hosts read the mail and sign off with contact information.
